Title: A Reason Contesting SHOULD Have a Heavy Penalty?

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
Haze came up with this, in another thread. He was responding to a
specific proposal by Damnans, but I think it is generally applicable
to the question of whether contesting SHOULD be lest costly than it is
now:

Librarian wrote:
> Haze wrote:
> > On Aug 25, 5:42 am, Damnans <damnansv...@ono.com> wrote:
<snip>
> >> So here is my proposal:
> >> A contested vampire is still controlled by any Methuselahs who put him
> >> or her into play.
> >> A contested vampire untaps as normal during his or her controllers'
> >> untap phase.
> >> The controler of a contested vampire burns 1 pool or taps that vampire
> >> during his or her untap phase (i.e., the OLD infernal penalty).
> >> If the contested vampires share the same title as any other contested
> >> vampire or another ready vampire, then the title becomes contested as well.

<snip>

> > While this kind of rule change makes everyone nice and happy in the
> > case of an accidental contesting, what does it do against intentional
> > contesting? Me and a buddy could make a superstar vampire deck, and go
> > to a tournament with each of us playing an identical copy. If we're
> > ever at the same table, oh well that's only 1 pool a turn.
> > Or let's say we're 5 people doing this, and the deck is strong enough
> > against the metagame so all 5 get in the finals...
>
> > As I've heard, this "team attack" is actually how some MtG players
> > enter tournaments.
>
> That's known as collusion, and is illegal.

I'm not sure that's collusion. It is not, as far as I know, illegal
to play a deck someone else designed. Nor do I see how these players
are gaining much advantage out of their willingness to play the exact
same deck at the exact same tournament. There is merely less of a
penalty. It might be collusion if players coordinate their crypts so
they DON'T contest. It is hardly collusion if they shrug their
shoulders and say "who cares if we contest". Their crime has less to
do with collusion and more to do with being too lazy (or incompetent)
to design their own tournament-level deck.

But that does bring us to another issue. It is more in keeping with
the spirit of the game if each player comes with his own unique deck
(preferably one that he designed himself). The severity of the
contesting rule DOES tend to enforce this.

I think the "team attack" being referred to involves a group of
players picking a deck they think will, overall, be very good against
the field, and all playing that deck, (and here's the important part)
WITH the "team" mindset of sharing the prizes and working to make sure
that, wherever they have a chance to influence it, one of their own
gets to the finals and has a good shot to win. *That* is how I read

reference, though; it's just what I interpreted those statements as,
based on how some serious MtG players I knew used to approach
tournaments.

I feel that a rules set that encourages 4 buddies who travel to a
tournament to each bring their own separate deck (even if its a deck 3

rule that makes it feasible for all 4 to bring the same new secret

needs it?

forbidden by the tournament-organizing body and in VTES they are. The
team-attack thing is about maximizing a team's chances to get *a*
winner and spreading that wealth around a little better among the
skilled braintrust.

contestation, but neither of those has anything to do with what's

want to put someone on the team who's not pulling their weight - and
the deck often has trouble against itself even if it's good against
the metagame).

the competitive MtG folks I know/knew.

I think that if it were in the "spirit of the game" to reward
creativity or variety then we would contest archetypes or deck types.
Because when 5 people are at the same table and every single one of
them has S&B with bounce there's no much variety there, and I've seen
it, more than once. Well, yeah, maybe one of them has Korah and
Dolphin Black in it, the other has Lord Fianna and Morel and the other
has Jason the World's Voice and Quentin King, etc, etc, but for the
most part they're just playing Kindred Spirits, Telepathic
Misdirection, Eyes of Chaos and lots of stealth.

players bringing the same deck to a tournament, because many players
already do so but with different vampires. Why? Because that archetype
wins tournaments. Maybe we don't like it but it happens and if we are
willing to punish people that brings the same vampire to a tournament
even if they are doing different things with it or using different
disciplines then we would be punishing the same creativity that the
rule supposedly exists to reward, encourage, etc. And all because,
maybe, just maybe, they are bringing the same deck, and because maybe,
just maybe they didn't come up with the idea but copied it from
somewhere.

I've seen players doing "team attack" playing entirely different decks
to help each other get to the finals not because they "share" the
prizes right away but because it is better to have their friend having
those cards that are easier to borrow or trade from or just because
they're friends. And we don't see anything punishing them, not even
this rule whose existence would be justified by this anti-team attack
nature.

For all of this, IMHO this isn't a very good reason for not having the
rules changed.

I disagree. The game, in its current form, and in part by its very
nature, does indeed reward these things in different degrees.

One factor is that the player who relies on what has worked before may
find his strategy more likely to be anticipated to varying degrees, or
"metagamed against" or whatever.

Another is the fact that each player must generally construct decks
out of his own collection. This limits his ability to construct decks
based on other people's collections. (Arguably, the PURPOSE of this
rule is to tempt players to buy more cards, but it still has other
effects).

Finally, a player who DOES find the cards necessary to construct
another person's deck may be selling himself short, by ignoring
opportunities that his own collection presents, or by ignoring
variations in the local playgroup metagame or local tournament
metagame.

> [...] nor should it try to distinguish between them (as that is impossible), [...]

I'm not sure what sort of proposal you are arguing against; but I
doubt anyone has proposed it.

> [...] nor do any of the current proposals for

> rules changes affect the balance between creativity and resourcefulness.

Maybe true, depending on what you mean by those categories.

However, any reduction of the severity of the contesting rule will
likely affect local play groups. If we re-define "creativity" to mean
"creativity and/or resourcefulness in constructing decks original to
the local playgroup" as distinct from "imitating each-other's decks",
then that balance will indeed be affected.

It can also affect the tournament scene. Suppose one of the members
of this local playgroup, having found a way to abuse a card from the
latest card-set, secretly comes up with what he believes to be an uber-
powerful deck design, with which he plans to make a surprise splash at
the next tournament. His fellow players (the only ones so far in on
the secret) are less likely to join him in going to the tournament
with the same deck, in part because they fear contesting at the
tournament, and in part because, again due to the danger of
contesting, they never got around to putting the deck together in the
context of their local playgroup.

I don't think we should ignore the potential effect of rules changes
on local playgroup behavior. Local playgroups are the core of the
game, and the basic source from which tournament players are derived.
